title: The first computer bug was a real moth

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: A real moth jammed a computer.
beats.on_screen_text: A real moth jammed a computer

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: You'd think a computer bug is just a word. A glitch, somewhere in the code.

elements.text: Bug = just a word for a glitch?

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: Nope. September ninth, 1947. Harvard's Mark II computer hits an error, and the operators find a moth caught in a relay.

elements.text: Harvard Mark II: a moth caught in a relay

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: Okay, but why write it down? Because engineers already called faults bugs. Edison used the word in 1878. So they taped the moth into the logbook and wrote: First actual case of bug being found.

elements.text: "First actual case of bug being found."

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: And the logbook, moth and all, is kept at the Smithsonian. No way. Really.

elements.text: The logbook, moth and all, is kept at the Smithsonian

claims.claim: A real moth got caught in a relay of a computer and caused an error (hook: "A real moth jammed a computer"; on screen: "Bug = an actual insect").
claims.source: Computer History Museum, This Day in History, September 9: the moth was "caught between the relay contacts of the Harvard Mark II computer" https://www.computerhistory.org/tdih/september/9/ ; Wikipedia, Software bug: "operators traced an error in the Mark II to a moth trapped in a relay." https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug
claims.note: "Jammed" is Blink's word for a moth caught between relay contacts causing an error; the sources say "caught" and "trapped".

claims.claim: It happened on September 9, 1947, on the Harvard Mark II computer (on screen: "9 September 1947", "Harvard Mark II: a moth caught in a relay").
claims.source: Computer History Museum, This Day in History, September 9 (1947): "Harvard Mark II computer in Cambridge, Massachusetts" https://www.computerhistory.org/tdih/september/9/
claims.note: Wikipedia's Software bug article says only "in about 1947"; the exact day is from the Computer History Museum.

claims.claim: Engineers already used the word "bugs" for faults before 1947; Thomas Edison used it in a letter in 1878 (on screen: "Edison writes 'bugs'" 1878, "Moth in the Mark II" 1947).
claims.source: Wikipedia, Software bug: Edison "wrote the following words in a letter to an associate in 1878": "'Bugs'—as such little faults and difficulties are called—show themselves" (letter to Puskas, 13 November 1878) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug ; Computer History Museum: the term originated "with Thomas Edison in the 1800s" https://www.computerhistory.org/tdih/september/9/
claims.note: The episode title says "first computer bug"; the script makes clear the word is older and this was the first actual insect.

claims.claim: The operators taped the moth into the computer's logbook and wrote "First actual case of bug being found."
claims.source: Computer History Museum, This Day in History, September 9: "They taped the dead moth into the logbook for the computer." One team member wrote "First actual case of bug being found" https://www.computerhistory.org/tdih/september/9/ ; Wikipedia, Software bug (same annotation) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug

claims.claim: The logbook with the moth is kept at the Smithsonian (National Museum of American History).
claims.source: Wikipedia, Software bug, reference for the logbook: "National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug ; Smithsonian object record "Log Book With Computer Bug" https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_334663 (the page refused automated access, so it was not read directly)
claims.note: Confirmed only through Wikipedia's citation; the Smithsonian page itself could not be opened by the fetch tool. The script does not say the logbook is on display.

publish.title: The first computer bug was a real moth
publish.description: In 1947 a moth got caught in a relay of Harvard's Mark II computer. The operators taped it into the logbook as the first actual bug ever found.
